newsitem.title: USA: Ease Americans' fear of death, study says.
newsitem.headline: Ease Americans' fear of death, study says.

text.p: Dying in American often hurts more than it should and could be improved with better pain management, training for doctors and drug law reform, the U.S Institute of Medicine reported Wednesday.
Researchers also said the medical profession, politicians and media could help relieve Americans' fear of death and misconceptions about dying by taking the issue "out of the closet."

"People in this country need to learn how to talk realistically about the end of life," said Dr Christine Cassel of New York's Mt. Sinai Medical Centre, who led the study, "Approaching Death: Improving Care at the End of Life."

"Public leaders and the media often ignore or distort the reality of dying with the resulting combination of fear, misinformation and oversimplification leading many to conclude that misery is inescapable," she said at a news conference.

Dr Joanne Lynn, director of George Washington University's Centre to Improve the Care of the Dying, said the media emphasis on spectacular death and dramatic medical resuscitations meant the everyday realities of dying as experienced by most people went largely unexplored.
"We have to start telling one another stories of good dying, stories about life well worth living right up to its last moments. It needs to come out of the closet," she said.

As a more practical matter, the report recommended changes in the way doctors and nurses were trained to overcome the cultural barriers raised by a medical profession that treated death as a failure of medicine.

"Medical schools and all clinical training programmes should ensure that practitioners have the knowledge and skills needed to care appropriately for dying patients ... scientific and clinical knowledge are important, but so are compassion, communication ability, experience and thoughtful reflection on the meaning of death,"it said.

The researchers noted that American medicine was more interventionist compared to other countries, with generally higher rates of surgery, diagnostic tests and life-prolonging procedures, and concluded that a "technological imperative" seemed to drive medical practice, including care of the dying.

The report recommended doctors, nurses and other health professionals commit themselves to better pain management and urged the reform of drug prescription laws and policies that impeded the effective use of painkillers such as morphine.

"Patients and their families should not suffer needlessly. Their wishes regarding care should be respected," it said, noting that 40 to 80 percent of those with cancer and AIDS reported inadequately treated pain.
